sources.title: Tiyo Soga (Q4426675), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-13): English label 'Tiyo Soga', description 'South African cleric and journalist (1829-1871)', instance of human, born 1829, died 12 August 1871, occupations including priest, journalist and translator. No Korean label or Korean Wikipedia article exists. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Christopher C. Lowe, 'Soga, Tiyo', Dictionary of African Christian Biography (reprinted from The Encyclopaedia Africana Dictionary of African Biography, vol. 3, 1995; read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: first ordained African minister in South Africa; born at Mgwali, seventh of 39 children of a counsellor to the Xhosa chiefs Ngqika and Sandile; Lovedale at 15; Scotland with William Govan in 1846; baptised, then catechist and interpreter; second Scottish period from 1851 (Glasgow University and the United Presbyterian Theological Hall); ordained December 1856; married Janet Burnside in February 1857; Mgwali mission 1857-67 and then Tutura at the request of the Gcaleka chief Sarili, where he died aged 42 of a throat ailment worsened by overwork; hymns, prayers and translations; sat on the board producing a more scholarly Xhosa Bible; first part of The Pilgrim's Progress published 1867; articles in Indaba on Xhosa proverbs, customs and legends; discrimination suffered with his wife, and a life that 'reflects the ironies and limits of African choices as white power grew'. Reference-work biography, balanced in tone; it says he translated 'the greatest part of the New Testament himself', which the board record in Chalmers does not support, so that claim is not used.

Willem Saayman, 'Soga, Tiyo', Dictionary of African Christian Biography (reproduced from Biographical Dictionary of Christian Missions, Eerdmans 1998; read in full). Short missiological entry: first black South African ordained to the Christian ministry (Glasgow, 1856), minister at Mgwali and then Tutura, a missionary approach 'typical of the time' concentrating on preaching and rudimentary teaching, but with a stronger interest than most in the healing dimension of mission. Independent academic voice that does not treat him as an exceptional mission strategist.

John A. Chalmers, 'Tiyo Soga: A Page of South African Mission Work' (Edinburgh: Andrew Elliot, 1877; Internet Archive full text, with his journal and letters; read the chapters on his literary labours and the Bible translation board in full and searched the rest). PRIMARY BIOGRAPHY BY A FRIEND AND MISSION COLLEAGUE, so admiring and partly drawn from Soga's own letters: his journal entry of 21 November 1866 finishing the first part of The Pilgrim's Progress, his letters on the interdenominational Board of Translators that began the Gospels in April 1869, the lost notebooks on Xhosa fables, customs and chiefs' genealogies, and his remarks to his children. Used for dates and his own words, never as an independent verdict.

John S. Ross, 'Sound the Trumpet: An introduction to the life and ministry of Tiyo Soga, 1829-1871', Haddington House Journal 2010 (read in full). Church-historian article by a Free Church minister who works on Eastern Cape mission history; it treats Chalmers as the primary source and Donovan Williams's 1978 biography and 1983 edition of Soga's journal as the scholarly base. Used for the sequence of events: threats at Uniondale over circumcision, the refused interpreter's post, the 1850-56 Glasgow studies, famine relief at Mgwali in 1857-58, the church built by 1862, fund-raising addresses, the 1865 'Defensor' letter to the King William's Town Gazette, and his last illness. Devotional in tone; Soga is described as a Christian first.

A. C. Jordan, 'Towards an African Literature IV: The Dawn of Literature among the Xhosa', Africa South, 1958 (reproduced by South African History Online; read in full). Independent literary history by a University of Cape Town lecturer in Bantu languages: names Soga the leading contributor to the newspaper Indaba, calls his translation Uhambo lo Mhambi 'excellent' with an influence on Xhosa 'almost as great' as the Authorized Version on English, notes his short stories, essays and hymns and the influence on younger writers, and states that W. W. Gqoba was 'unquestionably more talented' while Soga had the wider education. Critical voice on how much weight to give him.

Yvonne Surtees (compiler), 'Mgwali Mission and Tiyo Soga (c. 1829-1871)', Toposcope (Rhodes University / Albany Museum local-history journal; read in full). Heritage-trail account compiled from Donovan Williams's edition of his journal and other secondary works: Mgwali revived after the 1850 war, a title deed and further land grants for education, funds raised for the stone church because the Missionary Society doubted it was worth the cost, five schools including a boarding school for girls, 400-500 residents, the 1860 visit of Prince Alfred, the move to Thuthurha in 1868, the plaque inscription, his reconciling of Xhosa values with Western civilisation, and the later history of the mission as a site of resistance to forced removals. Heritage text, admiring; its 'firsts' and 'Black Consciousness' claims are not carded.

M. Hirst, 'Famous Firsts: The Soga family', Imvubu (newsletter of the Amathole Museum, Qonce) 16:2, 2004 (read in full). Museum newsletter drawing on Chalmers and Williams: his birth at Gwali in 1829, the decision not to circumcise him, his wide reading in Scotland and attraction to Bunyan, at least seven hymns in Incwadi Yamaculo (1864) and eight articles in Indaba, his 1865 exchange with Chalmers about the Xhosa's supposed doom, his preacher's throat and a doctor's advice in 1865 to resign that he did not follow, and his sons' careers. Its date for the second part of Pilgrim's Progress (1929, by his son) is a known discrepancy and is not used.

Sandiswa L. Kobe, 'Thinking Africa through Soga's black spirituals: A theological reflection', HTS Teologiese Studies / Theological Studies 80(2), 2024 (open access; read in full). Black-theology reading of two hymns that recounts later scholars' contested views of Soga (conflicted 'two worlds' minister in one reading, an assimilated 'model' missionary convert in another), quotes his Indaba call to record Xhosa history and customs in writing, and notes that one hymn is ascribed to him in the Presbyterian hymnbook but to 'G.S.' in the Methodist one. Interpretive and modern; used only for contested reception and hymn-attribution caution, never as behavioural evidence.

persistence.rationale: [src_soga_ross, src_soga_hirst, src_soga_dacb_lowe, src_soga_chalmers, src_soga_surtees | 1850-1871 | church-history article, museum newsletter, reference biography, colleague biography, heritage account] After the Uniondale station was burned in the 1850 war he returned to Glasgow to finish ministerial training despite a struggle with the studies (Ross, Surtees); at Mgwali he had 'preacher's throat' and in 1865 a doctor advised him to resign, which he did not follow (Hirst), and he finished the Pilgrim's Progress translation 'my fingers aching with writing' in 1866 (Chalmers journal); the DACB entry says he died at 42 of a throat ailment exacerbated by overwork. Several separate episodes, but most come from the Chalmers-Williams family. SOURCE-FAMILY CHECK: lowered from 74 / 0.60 to 72 / 0.56 because Ross, Hirst and Surtees all rest on Chalmers and Williams; only the DACB entry gives the overwork independently.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_soga_dacb_lowe, src_soga_ross, src_soga_chalmers, src_soga_jordan | 1848-1871 | reference biography, church-history article, colleague biography, literary history] Declined a well-paid government interpreter's post to complete ministerial training so that he could preach to his own people (Ross, from Chalmers); relief work, appeals to Scottish churches and burial of the dead at Mgwali during the famine of 1857-58 (Ross); translated, wrote hymns and recorded Xhosa lore for a Xhosa readership (Chalmers, Lowe, Jordan); Lowe says he 'strove to work for the good of his countrymen as he saw it'. The purposes are mostly stated by his friend and by later admirers. SOURCE-FAMILY CHECK / SELF-CALIBRATION: lowered from 72 / 0.58 via 70 / 0.54 to 68 / 0.52 because the motives rest on Soga's letters as presented by Chalmers and on retrospective summaries.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_soga_ross, src_soga_hirst, src_soga_dacb_lowe, src_soga_kobe | 1865-1870 | church-history article, museum newsletter, reference biography, theological article] Writing as 'Defensor' in the King William's Town Gazette in 1865 he challenged his friend Chalmers's claim that the Xhosa were doomed to extinction, arguing from scripture and from land policy (Ross, Hirst); Lowe says he was adamant in rejecting racialist characterisations of black people; in 1870 he wrote that he had no faith in a translation made by one translator or by someone who learned the language after the age of 17, and that the board would let Xhosa idiom, not English, set the text (Chalmers, his own letters). Against this, the same sources and later scholars (De Kock as reported by Kobe) read him as firmly within missionary orthodoxy and a 'model' convert, and he shared the mission assumption that Christian civilisation should be the way forward. SOURCE-FAMILY CHECK / SELF-CALIBRATION: lowered from 70 / 0.56 via 68 / 0.52 to 66 / 0.50 because the dispute is reported by Chalmers's circle and the orthodoxy reading is a real counter-voice.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_soga_ross, src_soga_surtees, src_soga_dacb_lowe | 1849-1865 | church-history article, heritage account, reference biography] At Uniondale he kept to his convictions after Xhosa fathers withdrew their sons from his school over his not being circumcised and his house was broken into (Ross); he and his wife faced loudly expressed disapproval in Cape Town and Port Elizabeth and 'resolutely refused to be troubled' (Ross, Surtees, Lowe); in 1865 he answered Chalmers under a pseudonym, and the friends' differences 'did not produce personal ill will' (Ross). Separate episodes of enduring hostility, but his responses were firm rather than confrontational, so the lean is modest. SOURCE-FAMILY CHECK: lowered from 60 / 0.50 (strong_inference) to 58 / 0.46 (inference) because the Uniondale account is from the Chalmers-Williams family and the Defensor letter was pseudonymous and collegial.

collaboration.rationale: [src_soga_chalmers, src_soga_ross, src_soga_surtees | 1857-1871 | colleague biography, church-history article, heritage account] He sat on the interdenominational Board of Translators of seven denominations from 1869, working through the Gospels session by session and, with Bryce Ross, composing the Xhosa text of agreed renderings (Chalmers, his own letters; Ross); at Mgwali he built the first mud church with his colleague Robert Johnston, taking turns at English and Xhosa services, and was saddened and discouraged when Johnston left (Ross); his hymns and Indaba contributions also fed a shared Xhosa-language press (Jordan). The harmony of the board is reported in his own letters. SOURCE-FAMILY CHECK: lowered from 66 / 0.54 to 64 / 0.50 because the board record is his own correspondence preserved by Chalmers.

persuasiveness.rationale: [src_soga_ross, src_soga_chalmers, src_soga_surtees | 1857-1862 | church-history article, colleague biography, heritage account] He raised the money for the new Mgwali church from supporters who doubted its value: Ross reports collections of about 13 pounds where 150 were hoped for, then over 200 pounds from his addresses in Port Elizabeth and 450 pounds in all from South African supporters, and Surtees says he raised a great portion of the funds against the Missionary Society's doubts; he preached in Presbyterian, Methodist, Anglican and Dutch Reformed congregations (Ross). The speaking is praised mostly by friends and the epitaph. SOURCE-FAMILY CHECK / SELF-CALIBRATION: lowered from 66 / 0.50 via 64 / 0.46 to 62 / 0.44; the outcomes are documented but the praise of his oratory is from Chalmers's circle and a funerary text.

adaptability.rationale: [src_soga_ross, src_soga_surtees, src_soga_dacb_lowe | 1846-1868 | church-history article, heritage account, reference biography] He moved between a Xhosa household, the multiracial Lovedale classroom, Glasgow (twice) and Eastern Cape mission stations, working in English and Xhosa and being a catechist, interpreter, student, minister and then station-builder at Mgwali (1857) and Tutura (1868, at Sarili's request); he arrived at Mgwali in the aftermath of the cattle-killing and changed his work to famine relief (Ross). Lowe and Surtees describe a life of two worlds that left him at times lonely. SOURCE-FAMILY CHECK: lowered from 68 / 0.54 to 66 / 0.50; the movements are documented but the 'two worlds' framing is the biographers' interpretation.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_soga_surtees, src_soga_ross, src_soga_dacb_saayman, src_soga_chalmers | 1857-1868 | heritage account, church-history article, missiological entry, colleague biography] At Mgwali he helped secure a title deed and further land grants for education, raised funds for the church, set up outstations and five schools including a boarding school for girls (Surtees); he vaccinated people against smallpox and kept a medicine chest (Ross) and Saayman notes an unusual interest in healing; he carried the Pilgrim's Progress translation, begun as a student, through the press in the midst of mission cares (Chalmers). The school and land details come from one heritage account. SOURCE-FAMILY CHECK: lowered from 70 / 0.56 to 68 / 0.52 because Surtees and Ross both draw on Williams and Chalmers.

curiosity.rationale: [src_soga_chalmers, src_soga_dacb_lowe, src_soga_jordan, src_soga_hirst, src_soga_kobe | 1850-1871 | colleague biography, reference biography, literary history, museum newsletter, theological article] He read widely during his Glasgow years (Prescott, Macaulay, Boswell) and was drawn to Bunyan (Hirst); he collected Xhosa fables, proverbs, customs and chiefs' genealogies in notebooks that were never completed (Chalmers) and published pieces on proverbs, customs and legends in Indaba (Lowe), and Jordan says he lived 'in a much larger world of ideas' than his contemporaries. Four partly independent accounts agree on the lore-gathering, none describes motivation. Kept after review: the lore-collecting is described by Chalmers, Lowe and Jordan from different standpoints.

mastery_orientation.rationale: [src_soga_ross, src_soga_chalmers, src_soga_jordan | 1844-1870 | church-history article, colleague biography, literary history] At Lovedale he reportedly rose to the top of every class but mathematics (Ross, from Chalmers); on the translation board he said he was 'very particular, I may almost say determined' to admit only pure idiomatic Xhosa and that a translator who learned the language after 17 could not equal a native speaker (Chalmers, his own letters); Jordan judges the Pilgrim's Progress version 'excellent'. SOURCE-FAMILY CHECK: lowered from 64 / 0.50 (strong_inference) to 62 / 0.46 (inference) because the class standing and the standards are both quoted from Chalmers and Soga's own letters and only Jordan is independent.

resourcefulness.rationale: [src_soga_ross, src_soga_surtees | 1857-1862 | church-history article, heritage account] With starving families arriving at Mgwali in 1857-58 he and his wife wrote to friends in Scotland for aid that churches there then supplied, and he built the first church with his own hands, learning to cut and fit glass; the funds for the larger church came from a mix of Port Elizabeth addresses, South African donors and Scottish friends. All of it comes from the Chalmers-Williams account. SOURCE-FAMILY CHECK: lowered from 62 / 0.46 to 60 / 0.42.

portrait.source: Albumen print photograph of Tiyo Soga (oval vignette, seated with a book), photographer anonymous, made in South Africa c. 1866 to before August 1871, tipped in as the frontispiece of John A. Chalmers, 'Tiyo Soga: A Page of South African Mission Work' (Edinburgh: Andrew Elliot, 1877) above a facsimile signature 'Tiyo Soga' in his own hand and facing the title page; held by the Rijksmuseum, Amsterdam (object RP-F-2001-7-367-1, photograph 94 x 58 mm; the whole book is RP-F-2001-7-367). The file is the photograph cropped from the museum's 5058 x 4126 pixel scan of the opening (cropped region 1082 x 1756 pixels) and downscaled to 616 x 1000, with no upscaling.
portrait.license: Public domain (Public Domain Mark 1.0 on the Rijksmuseum record, which states copyright 'Publiek domein'); 1860s photograph by an unknown photographer, published in Edinburgh in 1877

portrait.creator: Anonymous photographer (South Africa)

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: PLAUSIBLE (lead) / REPLACED BY THE SAME SITTER'S ORIGINAL: the lead, Commons 'Tiyo Soga - African nationalist politician of the Cape Colony.jpg' (659 x 900, uploaded 2011, author 'Anonymous', source only 'Photograph archive', tag PD-SOUTH-AFRICA), is a halftone reproduction of the same oval photograph with no holder, publication or date, so it was not used. The replacement is the original albumen print of that photograph, tipped in as the frontispiece of Chalmers's 'Tiyo Soga: A Page of South African Mission Work' (Edinburgh, 1877) above a facsimile signature 'Tiyo Soga', held by the Rijksmuseum (RP-F-2001-7-367-1). HOLDER RECORD READ (web page and linked-data record at hdl.handle.net/10934/RM0001.COLLECT.636381): maker 'photographer: anonymous', made in South Africa, dated ca. 1866 to in or before August 1871, albumen print 94 x 58 mm, note 'Foto op frontispice', inscription 'printed [...] Tiyo Soga' in the sitter's own handwriting, copyright 'Publiek domein', Public Domain Mark 1.0 on the image record; no restriction or discrepancy found (the record's only gap is the photographer's name). IDENTITY: the scan of the opening shows the vignette above the facsimile signature 'Tiyo Soga' and facing the title page of the biography of Tiyo Soga; the lead is the same photograph. Crop of the photograph from the 5058 x 4126 page scan (1082 x 1756 px region), downscaled to 616 x 1000, no upscaling. KIND likeness (lifetime photograph of the sitter). PREFLIGHT: QID VERIFIED LIVE (2026-11-13, Wikidata API) Q4426675 label 'Tiyo Soga', description 'South African cleric and journalist (1829-1871)', human, born 1829, died 12 August 1871; no Korean label or Korean Wikipedia page; no existing candidate with this slug or QID. REGION sub_saharan_africa, nationality ZA (as other South African candidates), era 19th_century. KOREAN NAME 티요 소가 is a transliteration chosen by the researcher (no Korean Wikipedia or Wikidata label exists) and needs a Korean reviewer check. ZERO POLITICS: scored on ministry, translation, hymns, writing and mission education only; the later 'Black Consciousness' and 'African nationalist' framings (Commons file title, Surtees, Kobe) are not scored, nor are his statements on race beyond the 1865 newspaper dispute with Chalmers. ATTRIBUTION: attributable (dated letters, journal, publications, and a documented board record). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Lowe, 'Soga, Tiyo', Dictionary of African Christian Biography (src_soga_dacb_lowe), with Jordan 1958 for the translation's literary weight. READ (8 sources besides Wikidata): Lowe and Saayman DACB entries (full), Chalmers 1877 (Internet Archive; read the literary-labours and translation-board chapters in full and searched the rest), Ross 2010 (full), Jordan 1958 (full), Surtees Toposcope (full), Hirst Imvubu (full), Kobe 2024 (full). Not opened: Williams, 'Umfundisi' (1978) and 'The Journal and Selected Writings' (1983), De Kock 1994, Cousins 1893. Britannica, a Biblical Training article and a South African History Online page were read for orientation and are not cited. A web-search result from a content-farm mirror site contained an embedded instruction aimed at the assistant; it was ignored and the site was not used. PERSPECTIVES: reference biographies (Lowe, Saayman); colleague biography from his own letters (Chalmers); church-history article (Ross); independent literary history (Jordan); heritage and museum accounts (Surtees, Hirst); modern theological critique (Kobe). SOURCE FAMILIES: only about four independent behavioural families exist (Chalmers/Williams and everything derived from them; Lowe/Encyclopaedia Africana; Saayman; Jordan); most scored episodes come from the Chalmers-Williams family, so no row exceeds 0.56 and none is documented. CONTRADICTIONS: Lowe says he translated 'the greatest part of the New Testament himself' while Chalmers shows a seven-denomination board with Soga and Bryce Ross composing the Xhosa text and only the Gospels done by 1871 (so the card says board work); dates for Mgwali (to 1867 or 1868), for the Pilgrim's Progress printing (1866 or 1867) and for the Chalmers-Defensor newspaper exchange differ between sources and the cards say 'finished 21 November 1866' and 'in 1865'; Hirst's 1929 date for the second part is a mistake about his son John Henderson Soga's later work and is not used; the hymn Wazidala iinto zonke is ascribed to him in one hymnbook and to 'G.S.' in another, so only the better-attested Lizalis' idinga lakho and the 1864 collection are carded. Surtees's 'first to formulate Black Consciousness' claim and Lowe's remark that he 'strove for the good of his countrymen as he saw it' are context, not scored. His loyalty to the Crown and colony (a DACB-C page not cited) is not scored. NOT SCORED: leadership_drive, risk_tolerance, discipline, belief_updating (no independent evidence beyond his own letters). SELF-CALIBRATION: 11 rows scored; concentration check lowered 10 rows (curiosity kept); self-calibration lowered 3 further (independent_thinking, impact_motivation, persuasiveness); see handback. MAJOR ACHIEVEMENT GATE: cards (1) Pilgrim's Progress translation, (2) first ordained African minister and the Mgwali and Tutura missions, (3) hymns, Indaba and the Bible board. Ethnographic collecting is not an achievement card because the notebooks were lost.
